nameStory: The "forget-me-not" name comes from a romantic medieval legend about a knight who fell into a river while picking these flowers for his beloved, calling out "forget me not!" as he drowned. The "bay" part of this species' name refers to its love of quiet, sheltered waters like those found in protected bays and coves.
description: Bay forget-me-not is a delicate, low-growing herb that produces tiny blue flowers with yellow centers. This modest plant typically grows 4-12 inches tall and has a sprawling habit, often forming loose mats near water. It's one of several forget-me-not species in New England, distinguished by its particularly small flowers and preference for wet areas where it may even grow partially submerged in shallow water.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale blue flowers, each about 1/8 inch across, with five rounded petals and bright yellow centers that fade to white with age. The flowers are notably smaller than other forget-me-nots and arranged in loose, curving clusters that unfurl like a fiddlehead.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly rough and hairy to the touch, arranged alternately along weak, often reclining stems. The leaves have a soft, grayish-green color and no teeth along their edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose, spreading tufts with weak stems that often trail along the ground or hang over the edges of streams and pond margins. The plant has a relaxed, almost drooping appearance compared to its more upright relatives.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces tiny, dark brown nutlets that are smooth and shiny, about the size of a pinhead. These develop in small clusters where the flowers once bloomed.

habitat: Look for bay forget-me-not in wet meadows, along stream banks, pond edges, and in shallow water of quiet bays and backwater areas. It thrives in mucky or sandy soils that stay consistently moist, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other wetland plants. This species is particularly fond of areas with fluctuating water levels.

seasonality.spring: Small blue flowers begin appearing in late spring, starting as tight coils that gradually unfurl. New leaves emerge bright green and soft.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs through early summer, with the characteristic tiny blue flowers most visible. Plants may continue flowering sporadically into late summer if conditions remain moist.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed production occurs. Foliage may persist but becomes less conspicuous as other wetland plants dominate the scene.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving little trace except perhaps some dried stems in protected areas.

funFact: Henry David Thoreau was particularly enchanted by this humble little flower, writing that it "hangs over the edge of the brook" and calling it "the more beautiful for being small and unpretending" - proving that even famous naturalists appreciated life's modest treasures.
confusionNotes: Bay forget-me-not is easily confused with water forget-me-not, but bay forget-me-not has distinctly smaller flowers and weaker, more trailing stems. Remember: "bay" means "baby" - the flowers are noticeably tinier than its more robust water-loving cousin.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name Myosotis literally means "mouse ear" in Greek, referring to the shape and fuzzy texture of the leaves. Despite the romantic legend, the actual origin of "forget-me-not" likely comes from the plant's persistent, memorable appearance once you learn to spot it.
compareHints: Among New England's forget-me-nots, bay forget-me-not stands out for having the smallest flowers and most relaxed growth habit. Water forget-me-not has larger, more vibrant blue flowers and sturdier stems, while wood forget-me-not prefers drier forest settings. The tiny flower size and wetland habitat make bay forget-me-not relatively easy to distinguish once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Water forget-me-not is distinguished from other forget-me-not species by its preference for wet habitats and its perennial, mat-forming growth habit.
Blue forget-me-not is the most rigid and unbranched of all New England forget-me-nots, with distinctly smaller flowers than its relatives.
Wood forget-me-not differs from water forget-me-not by preferring drier woodland soils versus wet areas, and it has a more compact growth habit.
Field forget-me-not differs from water forget-me-not by preferring dry, disturbed soil rather than wet areas, and having more pronounced patent hairs on its stems.
Unlike the common water forget-me-not which stays bright blue and grows in wet areas, changing forget-me-not prefers drier disturbed soil and shows its telltale color progression.
Among New England's forget-me-nots, early forget-me-not is the smallest and most easily overlooked.
